claims.text: Koji is grain cultured with koji mould.
Koji enzymes break starch into sugars and proteins into amino acids. Tiny cutters is an explanatory metaphor.
Koji amazake sweetness comes from rice starch acted on by koji-derived enzymes. Sake-lees amazake may be made with added sugar.

script.title: How Koji Turns Rice Starch into Sweetness | Japan Explained
script.description: Koji supplies enzymes that break down starch and protein. Koji amazake gets characteristic sweetness from enzyme action on rice starch; sake-lees amazake is a different preparation. No health or home-brewing advice. Original illustrative diagrams. #JapanExplained #Shorts

segments.text: Koji can make a rice drink sweet by breaking down its starch. The surprising part is where that sweetness comes from.
Koji is grain, such as steamed rice, cultured with a particular mould. It provides enzymes that help transform the food.
Think of those enzymes as tiny cutters. They break starch down into sugars. In koji amazake, that's what creates the drink's characteristic sweetness.
Other enzymes break proteins down into amino acids. So koji works on more than one kind of ingredient inside the grain.
But not every drink called amazake is made the same way. A version made with sake lees can have sugar added.
The takeaway: fermentation isn't just waiting. Koji supplies chemical tools that change what's already in the food.
